Financial reporting becomes more useful when you can see how revenue, profitability, and margins move together.

A trailing-twelve-month view can help reveal longer trends, while adjusted EBITDA and margin measures add context to the headline revenue number.

The Performance Overview page in my Financial Performance & Cash Flow Power BI Kit brings these measures together: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4595413257/power-bi-financial-dashboard-template-13

A consolidated financial result can hide meaningful differences between operating entities.

One entity might generate strong revenue but lower margins, while another contributes less revenue with stronger profitability. Looking beneath the total helps explain which parts of the business are driving performance.

Try comparing adjusted EBITDA margins across entities. Which differences deserve a closer look, and how have those relationships changed over time?

A profitable business still needs to know whether it can meet its upcoming cash obligations.

A 13-week cash forecast helps bring projected inflows, outflows, balances, and available credit into view. It gives financial performance a forward-looking perspective that historical results alone cannot provide.

My Financial Performance & Cash Flow Power BI Kit includes a cash forecast page: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4595413257/power-bi-financial-dashboard-template-13

A good financial dashboard should help people understand several connected questions about the business.

How profitable are operations? Which entities contribute most to performance? What does the near-term cash position look like? Each perspective helps make the overall picture more useful for planning and discussion.

For anyone involved in financial reporting, which do you find more challenging to explain to stakeholders: profitability trends or cash flow expectations?
